facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Hongshanornis was recovered in 2005 and is now held by the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen, recovered in 2005, is currently held by the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing.

facts.statement: Hongshanornis fossils were found in the Jianshangou fossil beds, which are dated to 124.6 million years ago.
facts.quote: It was found in the Jianshangou fossil beds, dated to 124.6 million years ago.

facts.statement: Adult Hongshanornis longicresta was about the size of a thrush, weighing approximately 50 grams with a wingspan of about 320 mm.
facts.quote: Hongshanornis longicresta was a small species, especially compared to other early ornithuromorphs (birds with a modern tail anatomy), about the size of a thrush, and adult specimens are estimated to have weighed about 50 g in life, with a wingspan of about 320 mm.

facts.statement: Researchers noted a unique bone at the end of the lower jaw in Hongshanornis that they compared to the predentary bone found in ornithischian dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The describers of Hongshanornis noted a unique bone in the end of the lower jaw which they equated with the beak-bearing "predentary bone" similar to the one found in ornithischian dinosaurs.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Hongshanornis possessed a beak, as some scientists argue its jaw bone lacks the characteristic pits and grooves found in early beaked birds.
facts.quote: However, other scientists have pointed out that the "predentary" (or, technically, mandibular symphysial ossification) of Hongshanornis lacks the characteristic pits and grooves associated with the beak in early beaked birds like Archaeorhynchus, and that the presence or absence of any beak is unclear.

facts.statement: Original describers suggested Hongshanornis had a large feathered crest, but this may be an artifact of preservation due to poor quality traces.
facts.quote: The original describers of Hongshanornis noted the apparent presence of a large feathered crest on the head, though the feather traces are poor quality and it may be an artifact of preservation.

facts.statement: A second specimen of Hongshanornis lacked long head feathers, showing instead feathers that became shorter near the snout.
facts.quote: A second specimen from different fossil beds did not have long feathers on the head, but rather showed feathers which became shorter closer to the snout.

facts.statement: The total wing area of Hongshanornis was 0.016 square meters.
facts.quote: The total wing area was 0.016 square meters.

facts.statement: The third toe was the longest among the toes of Hongshanornis.
Hongshanornis had at least 10 tail feathers, which is more than other primitive fan-tailed birds.
facts.quote: There were at least 10 tail feathers (rectrices), more than in other primitive fan-tailed birds.

facts.statement: A specimen of Hongshanornis preserved gizzard stones, suggesting an herbivorous diet.
facts.quote: One specimen of Hongshanornis preserved several gizzard stones (gastroliths) of various sizes, which is usually an indication of an herbivorous diet.

facts.statement: The absence of wing slotting suggests Hongshanornis tended to fly at relatively high speeds.
facts.quote: The absence of wing slotting would suggest that Hongshanornis tended to fly mainly at relatively high speeds.

facts.statement: Hongshanornis likely flapped continuously at low speeds and switched to bounding flight at higher speeds.
facts.quote: Given the overall wing shape and comparison to modern birds, Hongshanornis probably flapped continuously when flying at lower speeds, and switched to bounding flight (rapid flapping alternating with periods of ballistic forward motion with the wings partly folded) at higher speeds.

facts.statement: Hongshanornis is the namesake of the family Hongshanornithidae.
facts.quote: Hongshanornis is a member of the group Hongshanornithidae, to which it lent its name.

facts.statement: Hongshanornis is an ornithuromorph bird known from early Cretaceous lake deposits in the Yixian Formation of Inner Mongolia, China.
facts.quote: Hongshanornis is a genus of ornithuromorph birds known from early Cretaceous lake deposits of the Yixian Formation, Inner Mongolia, China.

facts.statement: Hongshanornis belongs to the family Hongshanornithidae.
The time range for Hongshanornis is from the Barremian to the Aptian, between 125.77 and 119.57 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Aptian (125.77 to 119.57 million years ago)
